title: Letter Writing
tagline: Composition · formal and informal letters: layout, tone and content

sourceNote.boardprep: All notes, model letters, phrases, vocabulary, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material. The names, addresses and organisations used in the models are fictional.

overview.intro: A letter is a piece of writing addressed to a particular person for a particular purpose. Formal letters go to editors, principals, officials and organisations, and they are polite, brief and businesslike. Informal letters go to friends and relatives and can be warm and chatty. This chapter shows the layout of each kind, the right tone, useful phrases and two model letters.

facts.label: Two kinds
facts.value: Formal (to editors, principals, officials) and informal (to friends and family)

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: Follow the layout your teacher or the question paper expects

facts.label: Formal tone
facts.value: Polite, precise, impersonal and to the point

facts.label: Informal tone
facts.value: Friendly, natural and personal, but still correct

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Follow the word limit given in the question

blocks.text: The first decision in any letter question is to decide who will read the letter and why. The reader and the purpose decide the layout, the tone and the choice of words.

items.meaning: Written to someone you do not know well or who holds an official position: an editor, a principal, a shop manager, an officer. Its purpose is usually to complain, request, apply, enquire or suggest. It has a subject line and a courteous, restrained tone.
Written to someone close to you: a friend, cousin, grandparent or sibling. Its purpose is to share news, describe an event, congratulate, thank or invite. It is written in a natural, friendly voice.

items: Read the question and underline who you are writing to, what has happened and what you want to say.
If the question gives you a name or an email address, use it. If it asks you to sign as a particular person, follow that instruction.
Do not use your own real name and address in a practice letter unless told to. Use an invented name or the name given in the question.
Follow the layout your teacher or the question paper expects. Layouts vary slightly, so be consistent within one letter.

blocks.text: A formal letter is usually arranged in the following order. Each part goes on its own line or lines, and there is a clear gap between the parts. Follow the layout your teacher or the question paper expects, as details such as the position of the date differ between schools.

items.meaning: Your address at the top, usually on the right or the left. Do not write your name here.
Written below the address, for example 12 August 2027. Use the same style throughout.
The name or designation of the person, then the organisation and its address, placed below the date.
The polite greeting, such as Dear Sir, Dear Madam or Dear Sir or Madam, followed by a comma.
A short, clear heading that states the topic in a phrase, not a sentence. Example: Subject: Irregular collection of garbage in Jasmine Road.
The message, in short paragraphs: the reason for writing, the details, and the request or suggestion.
The polite ending, commonly Yours faithfully when the letter begins Dear Sir or Madam, and Yours sincerely when it begins with the person's name.
Your signature and your name below the subscription. In a practice answer, write the name that the question gives or an invented one.

blocks.text: An informal letter leaves out the receiver's address and the subject line. Everything else keeps its place, though the tone is far more relaxed.

items: Sender's address, then the date, at the top.
Salutation with the person's first name or relationship, such as Dear Kabir, Dear Grandma or My dear Riya.
Body in two or three paragraphs: an opening line about the other person or their last letter, the main news, and a friendly closing paragraph.
Subscription that shows closeness, such as Yours affectionately, Your loving friend, With love or Yours ever.
Your first name below the subscription.

blocks.text: Even in an informal letter, keep your spelling, punctuation and sentences correct. Avoid text-message spellings such as 'u' for 'you' or 'gr8' for 'great'.

learn.title: Tone, register, paragraph plan and useful phrases

blocks.text: Register means the level of formality in your language. A formal letter avoids contractions (write 'I am' and not 'I'm'), slang and exclamation marks. An informal letter can use contractions, everyday words and a warm remark or two, but it should not ramble.

items: Paragraph 1 (formal): state the reason for writing in one or two sentences.
Paragraph 2 (formal): give the necessary details, facts, dates and the effect of the problem.
Paragraph 3 (formal): say exactly what you want done, and close with thanks or a request for a reply.
Paragraph 1 (informal): ask after the person and refer to their last message.
Paragraph 2 (informal): give the main news, in an order that a reader can follow.
Paragraph 3 (informal): end warmly with wishes, an invitation or a question that invites a reply.

items.meaning: I am writing to draw your attention to ...; I wish to bring to your notice ...; I am writing to enquire about ...
I would be grateful if you could ...; I request you to look into the matter; Kindly permit me to ...
I look forward to a prompt reply; Thanking you for your time and consideration; I shall be obliged if you will take action at your earliest convenience.
It was lovely to hear from you; You will never guess what happened; Do write soon and tell me all your news.

learn.title: Model formal letter: to a newspaper editor

blocks.text: Question: Write a letter to the editor of a newspaper about the irregular collection of garbage in your locality. The model below is an original BoardPrep sample of about 150 words in the body. All names and addresses are invented.

items: Sender's address: 27, Jasmine Road, Meadowpur
Date: 14 September 2027
Receiver's address: The Editor, The Meadowpur Courier, 5, Press Street, Meadowpur
Salutation: Dear Sir,
Subject: Irregular collection of garbage in Jasmine Road

blocks.text: Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the municipal authorities to the irregular collection of garbage in Jasmine Road.

For the past three weeks, the garbage van has visited our lane only twice. As a result, waste has piled up beside the park wall, stray animals scatter it across the road, and a foul smell reaches the houses nearby. Many children walk past this spot on their way to school, and residents fear that the rotting waste may spread disease, especially with the monsoon approaching.

I therefore request the authorities to restore the daily collection at once and to place covered bins near the park. A fixed schedule displayed on the lamp post would also help residents keep their waste ready in time. I shall be grateful if you will kindly publish this letter so that it receives prompt attention.

items: Subscription: Yours faithfully,
Signature and name: Rohan Mehra

learn.title: Model informal letter: to a friend

blocks.text: Question: Write a letter to a friend describing how your school celebrated its annual sports day. This is an original BoardPrep sample of about 100 words in the body, with invented names.

items: Sender's address: 9, Neem Colony, Meadowpur
Date: 3 December 2027
Salutation: Dear Kabir,

blocks.text: How are you? I hope your exams have gone well. I am sorry it has taken me so long to write, but our sports day kept everyone busy.

It was held last Saturday, and you would have loved it. My house won the relay after a nail-biting finish, and I finished second in the long jump, which I had never expected. The best moment came when our sports teacher, Mr. Rao, tripped on the ribbon and then bowed to the whole ground, and even the principal laughed.
Do come during the holidays and I will show you my medal. Write soon and tell me all your news.

items: Subscription: Yours affectionately,
Name: Arjun
Writing a subject line as a full sentence or forgetting it in a formal letter. Use a short phrase.
Including a subject line or the receiver's address in an informal letter, where they are not expected.
Mixing tones: using slang or 'Hey' in a formal letter, or stiff phrases such as 'I wish to inform you' in a letter to a friend.
Mismatching the salutation and the subscription. Dear Sir goes with Yours faithfully, Dear Kabir goes with a friendly close.
Writing your own name in the sender's address, or forgetting the date.
Long, unbroken paragraphs. Break the body into two or three short paragraphs.
Leaving out the purpose. State clearly what you want, such as an action, a permission or a reply.
Ignoring the word limit in the question, or repeating the same point in different words.

keyPoints: Decide the reader and the purpose first; they determine layout, tone and vocabulary.
A formal letter has a sender's address, date, receiver's address, salutation, subject line, body, subscription and signature.
An informal letter has no receiver's address and no subject line.
Match the salutation with the subscription, for example Dear Sir with Yours faithfully.
Follow the layout your teacher or the question paper expects, and stay consistent within one letter.
Use a formal register without slang or contractions in formal letters, and a warm but correct voice in informal ones.
Plan the body as three short paragraphs: reason, details, request or closing.
examFocus: Choosing the correct type of letter from the wording of the question.
Laying out all the parts of the letter in a sensible order.
Keeping the tone and register suitable for the reader.
Covering every point mentioned in the question, in organised paragraphs.
Accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation.
Staying within the word limit given in the question.

vocabulary.word: I wish to draw your attention to
vocabulary.meaning: a polite way of starting a complaint or a report about a problem
vocabulary.context: I wish to draw your attention to the broken street light outside our school.

vocabulary.word: I am writing to enquire about
vocabulary.meaning: a formal opening used to ask for information
vocabulary.context: I am writing to enquire about the dates of the inter-school quiz.

vocabulary.word: I would be grateful if you could
vocabulary.meaning: a courteous way of making a request
vocabulary.context: I would be grateful if you could extend the library hours during the exam week.

vocabulary.meaning: a formal way of saying you will be thankful if something is done
vocabulary.context: I shall be obliged if the repairs are completed before the monsoon.

vocabulary.meaning: as soon as it is possible for you
vocabulary.context: Please send me the fee receipt at your earliest convenience.

vocabulary.word: I look forward to a prompt reply
vocabulary.meaning: a closing line that shows you expect a quick answer
vocabulary.context: I look forward to a prompt reply, as the trip is only two weeks away.

vocabulary.word: through the columns of your newspaper
vocabulary.meaning: a phrase used in a letter to an editor, asking for the letter to be published
vocabulary.context: Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to suggest a cycle track on Station Road.

vocabulary.meaning: to investigate a problem and take suitable action
vocabulary.context: I request the manager to look into the matter and refund the amount.

vocabulary.meaning: a polite subscription commonly used when the letter begins Dear Sir or Dear Madam
vocabulary.context: The letter began Dear Madam, so it was closed with Yours faithfully.

vocabulary.meaning: a polite way of asking for permission
vocabulary.context: Kindly permit me to attend the workshop on the second of March.

questions.prompt: You are Nisha Rao of 42, Lotus Avenue, Meadowpur. Write a letter to the Principal of your school, Green Valley High School, requesting permission to organise a book donation drive on the school campus. Follow the word limit in the question.
questions.answer:
42, Lotus Avenue, Meadowpur
10 October 2027

The Principal
Green Valley High School
Meadowpur

Dear Madam,

Subject: Request for permission to hold a book donation drive

I am writing to request permission to organise a book donation drive in our school. Many students own storybooks they no longer read, while the library of the nearby village school has very few.

With the help of the Reading Club, we plan to collect books in the assembly hall on 25 and 26 October, sort them, and send them to the village school. Class monitors will keep a record of every donation.

I would be grateful if you could permit the drive and allow us to make an announcement in the morning assembly.

Yours faithfully,
Nisha Rao
questions.explanation: Marking checklist: sender's address and date (1); receiver's address (1); salutation (1); subject line as a short phrase (1); purpose stated in the opening (1); details of the plan (1); a clear request and polite close (1); matching subscription, signature and correct language (1).
questions.commonMistake: Writing the subject line as a long sentence or leaving out the date.

questions.prompt: Write a letter to your cousin, Meera, who lives in another city, inviting her to spend part of the summer holidays with you and describing what you have planned. Sign as Sameer of 18, Palm Road, Kaveripur.
questions.answer:
18, Palm Road, Kaveripur
2 May 2027

Dear Meera,

I hope you and everyone at home are well. I was delighted to hear that your exams have ended, and I have a request: please come and stay with us for a fortnight in June.

We have planned a lot. Grandpa has promised a day trip to the river, and we can go cycling every evening and finish the jigsaw puzzle we left half done last year. Mother will make your favourite mango pudding.

Do ask Aunt to send a message soon, so that we can book your train ticket in time.

Yours affectionately,
Sameer
questions.explanation: Marking checklist: address and date (1); friendly salutation (1); warm opening (1); clear invitation (1); planned activities covered in an ordered paragraph (2); friendly close asking for a reply (1); informal but correct language with no subject line or receiver's address (1).
questions.commonMistake: Adding a subject line and receiver's address to an informal letter.

questions.prompt: Loud music from a wedding hall near your house continues late into the night during the examination season. As a resident named Anil Kapoor of 6, Banyan Street, Kaveripur, write a letter to the editor of The Kaveripur Times, 2, Market Road, Kaveripur, expressing your concern. Follow the word limit in the question.
questions.answer:
6, Banyan Street, Kaveripur
20 February 2027

The Editor
The Kaveripur Times
2, Market Road
Kaveripur

Dear Sir,

Subject: Loud music late at night near Banyan Street

Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the loud music played at a nearby wedding hall until midnight.

Many students in our locality are preparing for examinations. The noise disturbs their sleep and study, and elderly residents and patients are troubled too.

I request the police and the municipal office to enforce a time limit for loudspeakers and to inspect the hall regularly. I look forward to prompt action.

Yours faithfully,
Anil Kapoor
questions.explanation: Marking checklist: all layout parts present and in order (2); appropriate subject line (1); formal opening naming the problem (1); reasons and effects given (2); specific request to the correct authority (1); polite closing, matching subscription and signature (1). Deduct for slang, contractions and rudeness.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming the wedding family in angry language instead of asking for a fair remedy.

questions.prompt: Spot four layout or tone errors in this formal letter to a shop manager: 'Ravi Nair, 3 Park Lane. Hey Manager, Subject - I am very angry that the cricket bat I bought from your shop last week has broken and I want my money back immediately!! Yours lovingly, Ravi.'
questions.answer: 1. The salutation 'Hey Manager' is too casual; it should be 'Dear Sir' or 'Dear Madam'. 2. The date and the receiver's address are missing. 3. The subject line is a long, angry sentence; it should be a short phrase such as 'Request for replacement of a defective cricket bat'. 4. 'Yours lovingly' is wrong for a formal letter; it should be 'Yours faithfully'. Also the tone is rude and the double exclamation marks are unsuitable.
questions.explanation: One mark for each correct error with its correction. Other valid points: the sender's address should sit at the top without the name, and the body should be split into short paragraphs.
questions.commonMistake: Only correcting the closing and ignoring the tone of the whole letter.

questions.prompt: Choose the more suitable subscription for each letter: (a) a letter beginning 'Dear Sir' to the Principal (Yours faithfully / Your loving friend); (b) a letter to a close friend (Yours faithfully / Yours affectionately); (c) a letter beginning 'Dear Madam' to a bank manager (Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully).
questions.answer: (a) Yours faithfully. (b) Yours affectionately. (c) Yours faithfully.
questions.explanation: Formal letters that begin Dear Sir or Dear Madam are commonly closed with Yours faithfully, while warm closes such as Yours affectionately belong to informal letters. Follow the convention your teacher or the question paper expects.
questions.commonMistake: Using an affectionate close in a formal letter.

questions.prompt: Rewrite each sentence in a suitable formal register for a letter to the Principal: (a) 'The fan in our class is broken, fix it.' (b) 'We want a day off for the match.' (c) 'Hope you'll say yes.' (d) 'Tell me soon.'
questions.answer: (a) I wish to bring to your notice that the ceiling fan in our classroom is not working; I request you to have it repaired. (b) We would be grateful if you could permit us a holiday on the day of the inter-school match. (c) I hope you will kindly consider my request favourably. (d) I look forward to a prompt reply.
questions.explanation: One mark for each rewrite that is polite, complete and free of contractions and slang. Any accurate, courteous wording is acceptable.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the command form, for example 'Please fix the fan', without softening the request.

questions.prompt: Which opening sentence is most suitable for a formal letter to a newspaper editor about the poor state of a public road?
options: Hi! You must see the road near my house!
Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the poor condition of Station Road.
I hope you are fine and enjoying the good weather.
The road is broken so fix it soon.
questions.answer: Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the poor condition of Station Road.
questions.explanation: It states the purpose at once and uses a courteous, formal register. The first is too casual, the third belongs to an informal letter and the fourth is a blunt command.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option that asks after the editor's health, which is a habit of informal letters.

questions.prompt: Which of these parts is normally included in a formal letter but left out of an informal letter?
questions.explanation: A formal letter carries a short subject line that announces the topic. An informal letter has a date, salutation and signature too, but no subject line and no receiver's address.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the salutation, which both kinds of letter have.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best subject line for a letter to a librarian asking for extra hours during exam week?
options: I want the library to stay open longer during the exams because we cannot study at home
Request for extended library hours during exam week
questions.answer: Request for extended library hours during exam week
questions.explanation: A good subject line is a short phrase that names the purpose and the topic. The first is a full sentence, the second is too vague and the fourth is a command that does not say why.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the longest option because it seems to give the most information.

questions.prompt: State four differences between a formal letter and an informal letter.
questions.answer: 1. A formal letter is addressed to an official or a stranger, while an informal letter is addressed to a friend or relative. 2. A formal letter has a receiver's address and a subject line, while an informal letter has neither. 3. A formal letter uses a polite, impersonal tone with no slang or contractions, while an informal letter uses a warm, personal tone. 4. A formal letter closes with Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely, while an informal letter closes with a friendly phrase such as Yours affectionately.
questions.explanation: One mark for each difference clearly stated. Other valid points: purpose, choice of words, and level of personal detail.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the same difference twice in different words, such as 'formal is serious' and 'informal is not serious'.
